workspace_links.description: Ask your data questions in plain English

nuggets.title: Welcome to the workshop
nuggets.markdown: You're about to build on Databricks with an AI coding agent at your side. Click **Claude Code** or **Codex** above to launch a terminal — your credentials are wired up automatically, nothing to paste.

nuggets.title: What makes an agent different from chat?
nuggets.markdown: A coding agent doesn't just suggest code — it runs commands, reads files, fixes its own mistakes, and iterates until the job is done. Treat it like a fast pair programmer: describe the *outcome* you want, not the steps.

nuggets.title: Pro tip: prompt for outcomes
nuggets.markdown: Instead of *"write a PySpark job"*, try *"create a pipeline that ingests the CSVs in /Volumes/main/default/raw into a Delta table, with data quality checks"*. Agents do their best work with a clear definition of done.

nuggets.title: Polly coordinates Claude and Codex
nuggets.markdown: Stock **Polly** is Omnigent's orchestrator. In this workshop it dispatches only Claude and Codex workers, each in its own worktree, so one agent can implement while the other reviews. Give Polly a clear task and ask it to report which worker did each part.

nuggets.title: Try it: what did that actually cost?
nuggets.markdown:
Build something small with **Polly**, then open the Omnigent app and read the session's token usage and per-model breakdown. Ask Polly to send one focused review to its other worker and compare three things: total tokens, how many turns each needed, and whether the review found something worth fixing.

Compare **tokens** rather than assuming an unpublished price is zero. Where the catalog publishes a price, Omnigent shows both.

nuggets.title: Unity Catalog: three-level naming
nuggets.markdown: Everything you create lives at `catalog.schema.object`. Ask your agent to put workshop tables in your assigned schema — governance, lineage and permissions come for free.

nuggets.title: The Databricks CLI is pre-authenticated
nuggets.markdown: Try `databricks current-user me` in any terminal. Your agent can use the full CLI and REST API as *you* — short-lived credentials rotate automatically in the background.

nuggets.title: Best practice: serverless first
nuggets.markdown: For new pipelines and SQL, serverless compute starts in seconds and scales to zero — no cluster babysitting. Ask your agent to default to serverless when it creates jobs or pipelines.

nuggets.title: Declarative pipelines do the heavy lifting
nuggets.markdown: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines handle retries, dependencies, and incremental processing from a few annotations. Ask your agent for *"a declarative pipeline with a bronze/silver/gold flow"* and compare it to hand-rolled Spark.

nuggets.title: Give your business users Genie
nuggets.markdown: AI/BI Genie lets anyone ask questions of governed data in plain English. Once your tables land in Unity Catalog today, they're one click away from a Genie space.

nuggets.title: Stuck? Let the agent debug itself
nuggets.markdown: Paste the error straight into the agent and say *"diagnose and fix"*. Agents are excellent at reading stack traces — and they learn the shape of your project as they go.

nuggets.title: You're using Lakebase 🐘
nuggets.markdown: Lakebase is **fully-managed Postgres built into Databricks** — your app gets a real OLTP database with zero infrastructure, branching for dev/test, and synced tables that flow straight into your lakehouse. No separate database vendor, one governance model.
nuggets.prompt: Add a Lakebase Postgres database to my app and store its state there.

nuggets.title: Unity Catalog is doing the governance for you
nuggets.markdown: Every table, model, and volume you just touched is governed in one place: permissions, lineage, audit, discovery. That's the difference between a demo and something your security team will approve.

nuggets.title: Genie: your tables, in plain English
nuggets.markdown: The data you're building can be handed to business users today — AI/BI Genie lets them ask questions in natural language with answers grounded in your governed tables. Zero dashboards to build first.
nuggets.prompt: Set up a Genie space over the tables we built so business users can query them in plain English.

nuggets.title: Declarative pipelines: you declare, Databricks operates
nuggets.markdown: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines handle orchestration, retries, incremental processing, and data quality enforcement from a few annotations. The pipeline you're building would be hundreds of lines of hand-rolled orchestration anywhere else.
nuggets.prompt: Add data quality expectations to my pipeline and show me what fails.

nuggets.title: Vector Search without the vector database
nuggets.markdown: Databricks Vector Search syncs embeddings straight from your Delta tables — no separate vector DB to run, govern, or pay for. Your RAG index inherits Unity Catalog permissions automatically.
nuggets.prompt: Create a Vector Search index over my data and wire up a simple RAG query.

nuggets.title: MLflow 3: observability for AI you can act on
nuggets.markdown: Every agent call you're tracing lands in MLflow — token costs, latencies, full traces, evaluation scores. It's the difference between 'the demo worked' and 'we know exactly how it behaves in production'.
nuggets.prompt: Enable MLflow tracing for what we're building and show me a trace.

nuggets.title: One endpoint, every frontier model
nuggets.markdown: Model Serving gives you Claude, GPT, Llama and your own models behind one governed, rate-limited, pay-per-token endpoint — the same one powering the agent in your terminal right now.

nuggets.title: Ship that app on Databricks Apps
nuggets.markdown: What you're building can be deployed as a Databricks App: serverless hosting, workspace SSO, governance built in. No Kubernetes, no separate auth, straight from code to a URL your team can open.
nuggets.prompt: Deploy what we've built as a Databricks App.

nuggets.title: AI/BI Dashboards on live lakehouse data
nuggets.markdown: Dashboards here query your governed tables directly — no extracts, no stale copies. Build one with your agent: *"create a dashboard showing the table we just built"*.
nuggets.prompt: Create an AI/BI dashboard for the table we just built.

nuggets.title: Lakeflow Jobs: scheduling included
nuggets.markdown: Anything you've built can run on a schedule with retries, alerts, and serverless compute — ask your agent to *"schedule this as a daily job"* and it's production-ready automation.
nuggets.prompt: Schedule what we built as a daily job with email notifications.

nuggets.title: Build complete — save your docs
nuggets.markdown: Your agent just finished a build. Ask it to generate handoff documentation — architecture spec, security review, Jira stories, test cases, and a build prompt — uploaded automatically to your Databricks Volume so you can share and revisit everything you built today.
nuggets.prompt: Please generate handoff documentation for what I just built and upload it to my Databricks Volume.

nuggets.title: Save your work before this environment goes away
nuggets.markdown:
This workspace is deleted after the workshop. Ask your agent for handoff docs — architecture, security review, Jira stories, test cases and a rebuild prompt — uploaded to your Databricks Volume so you can read them today.

**Didn't finish?** Ask anyway. The docs cover what you were heading towards and where it stopped, which is the version worth having when you pick it up again.
nuggets.prompt: We're wrapping up. Generate the handoff docs for this session — architecture, security review, Jira stories, test cases and a rebuild prompt — and upload them to my Databricks Volume. If we didn't finish something, document what we were going for and where it stopped rather than leaving it out.

nuggets.title: Take it with you — nothing here is saved
nuggets.markdown:
Everything in this environment is deleted at the end of the event: the terminal, the workspace folder your commits sync to, and the Volume your handoff docs go to. Committed is not the same as saved.

**Two ways to keep it:** push the repo to a git remote you own — your agent will walk you through it — or download the files you care about from your Databricks Workspace folder while the event is still running.
nuggets.prompt: I want to keep this work after the workshop. Walk me through pushing my project to a git remote I own, and tell me exactly what I should download before this environment is deleted.

nuggets.title: Keep building after today
nuggets.markdown: Everything you used today works in your own workspace — and you can have one **free, forever**: Databricks Free Edition takes two minutes to set up. Pair it with the free Customer Academy courses to keep the momentum.

nuggets.title: Your coach is waiting
nuggets.markdown: Open **Claude Code** and tell it what you'd like to build — in plain words, no syntax to learn. Not sure? Ask it to pick something good and build it for you.

nuggets.title: Idea: make the agent show its plan
nuggets.markdown: Before a big step, try *“explain your plan before doing anything”*. You'll learn how the agent thinks — and catch wrong turns before they happen.

nuggets.title: While you're thinking: add quality checks
nuggets.markdown: A great next prompt: *“add data quality expectations to my pipeline and show me what fails”*. Real pipelines earn trust with checks, not hope.

nuggets.title: Next step: see your data
nuggets.markdown: Your tables deserve a face. Ask your agent: *“create an AI/BI dashboard for the table we just built”* — it's one prompt away.

nuggets.title: There's real data already here 📊
nuggets.markdown: You don't have to make data up. There's a catalog of realistic industry data in this workspace — vehicles, customers, parts, transactions — ready to query. Your agent knows where it is.
nuggets.prompt: What demo data is available in this workspace? Show me the tables, then pick the most interesting one and build me something with it.

nuggets.title: Claim your certificate 🏆
nuggets.markdown: You built real things on Databricks today. Download your personalized certificate — with your stats: agent sessions, lines of code, resources created.

all.label: What can you do here?
all.prompt: What can you help me build on Databricks today? Give me three concrete options.

intro.label: Explore the workshop data
intro.prompt: Explore what data is available in this workspace and show me something interesting about it.

setup.label: Check my setup
setup.prompt: Run databricks current-user me and confirm my environment is ready to build.

build.label: Build my first pipeline
build.prompt: Create a declarative pipeline with a bronze/silver/gold flow over the workshop dataset, with data quality checks.

build.label: Make a dashboard
build.prompt: Create an AI/BI dashboard for the tables we have built so far.

build.label: Ship it as an app
build.prompt: Turn what we have built into a small Databricks App with a clean UI.

build.label: Compare model costs
build.prompt: Pick one small, self-contained task from what we're building — something a single sub-agent can finish and open a PR for. State the task back to me in one sentence so I can reuse it word for word, then do it. When you're done, report how many sub-agents you dispatched, which model each one ran, and how many turns each took. Don't change any worker's model: I want to see what this tier costs as configured.

wrap.label: Sum up what I built
wrap.prompt: Summarize everything we built today, commit any uncommitted work, and tell me how to keep going in my own workspace.

wrap.label: Save my work
wrap.prompt: We're wrapping up. Generate the handoff docs for this session — architecture, security review, Jira stories, test cases and a rebuild prompt — and upload them to my Databricks Volume. If we didn't finish something, document what we were going for and where it stopped.

wrap.label: Where did I get stuck?
wrap.prompt: Walk back through this session: what was I trying to do, what worked, and what blocked me? Be specific about the errors, and tell me what I'd need to get past them in my own workspace.

wrap.label: Take my work with me
wrap.prompt: I want to keep this work after the workshop. Walk me through pushing my project to a git remote I own, and tell me exactly what I should download before this environment is deleted.

wizard_intent_labels.business_problem: Solving a real problem from work
wizard_intent_labels.evaluation: Seeing whether Databricks can do this

ideas.label: Find the parts that fail early
ideas.outcome: A page ranking parts by how often they fail per 1,000 vehicles
ideas.prompt: Build me a dashboard ranking parts by warranty claims per 1,000 vehicles fitted, using automotive_mobility.parts360. Show the worst 20, break them down by supplier and by affected model, and flag any part where the rate is rising. Prepared tables: automotive_mobility.warranty_claims.

ideas.label: Spot vehicles heading for a breakdown
ideas.outcome: A model that flags vehicles likely to need unplanned work
ideas.prompt: Train a model that predicts which vehicles are heading for an unplanned repair. Use automotive_mobility.telematics_events for behaviour and fault codes, automotive_mobility.vehicle360 for age and service history, and warranty claims as the outcome to learn from. Show me which signals mattered most. Prepared tables: automotive_mobility.dtc_codes, automotive_mobility.warranty_claims.

ideas.label: Ask questions about the fleet in plain English
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can type a question and get an answer from the data
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over automotive_mobility.vehicle360 and automotive_mobility.customer360 so I can ask questions about the fleet in plain English. Give it good descriptions and a few example questions to start from.

ideas.label: Clean the prepared telematics data
ideas.outcome: An incremental pipeline cleaning seeded telemetry into a queryable table
ideas.prompt: Build an incremental pipeline over automotive_mobility.telematics_events. Check timestamps, vehicle identifiers and impossible readings, and show which rows failed validation. Use the prepared table; do not assume a raw-file volume exists.

ideas.label: See which customers are drifting away
ideas.outcome: A page listing customers who still own a car but stopped coming in
ideas.prompt: Build an app over automotive_mobility.customer360 showing current vehicle owners who have not returned for service in over 18 months. Show the existing service_defection_flag and next_best_action. Filter by state and rank by lifetime service spend.

ideas.label: Track how a recall is going
ideas.outcome: A live view of which vehicles still have outstanding recall work
ideas.prompt: Track completed versus outstanding recalls using automotive_mobility.recall_campaigns and automotive_mobility.campaign_vehicles. Join automotive_mobility.vehicle360 for model and automotive_mobility.customer360 for owner state. Label state as current owner location, not recall service location.

ideas.label: Stop running out of the parts you need
ideas.outcome: A page showing which parts are about to run out and where
ideas.prompt: Build an app that flags parts at risk of stocking out: compare on-hand and on-order against the last 12 months of consumption in automotive_mobility.parts360, weight it by how badly the part has run out before, and show me the worst locations. Prepared tables: automotive_mobility.parts_inventory.

ideas.label: See how the electric fleet is charging
ideas.outcome: A view of charging behaviour across the electric and hybrid vehicles
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard on automotive_mobility.charging_sessions joined to automotive_mobility.vehicle360: energy delivered over time, how it splits across charger speeds, cost per kWh, and which models charge most. Only BEV and PHEV vehicles have sessions, so make that explicit.

ideas.label: Work out which part actually ships today
ideas.outcome: A lookup that follows a part through every replacement to the current one
ideas.prompt: In the automotive_mobility.parts table, superseded_by forms chains rather than single hops, so the current part number can be several replacements away. Write the query that walks a part to the end of its chain, then wrap it in a small lookup app. automotive_mobility.parts360 already has the answer resolved, so check yourself against it.

ideas.label: See which stores are about to run out
ideas.outcome: A page showing stores at risk of running out of their best sellers
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard showing which retail.stores are about to run out of stock: compare daily inventory against how fast each product is selling, and rank by the revenue at risk. Prepared tables: retail.inventory_daily, retail.products.

ideas.label: Find what people buy together
ideas.outcome: A list of product pairs that sell together more often than chance
ideas.prompt: Work out which retail.products get bought together from the order lines, score the pairs so coincidence does not dominate, and show me the strongest combinations by category. Prepared tables: retail.orders, retail.order_items.

ideas.label: Give store managers their own page
ideas.outcome: A small app a store manager can open to see just their store
ideas.prompt: Build a phone-friendly store manager app using retail.stores and retail.inventory_daily for stock. Join retail.orders to retail.order_items for sales totals and a previous-week comparison. Use the latest seeded dates and disclose the synthetic data period instead of implying live sales.

ideas.label: Catch fraudulent transactions
ideas.outcome: A model that scores transactions and explains why it flagged them
ideas.prompt: Train a fraud detection model on the financial_services.transactions table using financial_services.fraud_labels as the ground truth. Deal with how rare fraud is, show me precision and recall rather than just accuracy, and tell me which features drove the flags.

ideas.label: Ask where the money is going
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask spending questions in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over financial_services.transactions, financial_services.merchants and financial_services.customers so I can ask about spending patterns in plain English, with example questions to get started.

ideas.label: Build the transaction pipeline properly
ideas.outcome: A clean, tested flow from raw transactions to something reportable
ideas.prompt: Build a bronze/silver/gold pipeline over the financial_services.transactions data with real data quality checks — no negative amounts, no financial_services.transactions on closed financial_services.accounts, no duplicate ids — and show me what it caught.

ideas.label: Predict who is likely to come back
ideas.outcome: A model flagging patients at risk of readmission
ideas.prompt: Build a model predicting 30-day readmission from healthcare.encounters, patient history and healthcare.diagnoses. Be careful not to leak anything from after discharge, and tell me which factors mattered. Prepared tables: healthcare.patients.

ideas.label: See where the pressure is
ideas.outcome: A view of demand by department, day and time
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard showing where demand is concentrated: healthcare.encounters by department, day of week and hour, average length of stay, and which healthcare.providers are carrying the most.

ideas.label: Ask questions about claims
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask about claims and costs in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over healthcare.claims and healthcare.diagnoses so I can ask about cost and volume in plain English. This is synthetic data, so say so in the space description.

ideas.label: Spot work orders at risk of defects
ideas.outcome: A demo model estimating defect risk from earlier machine readings
ideas.prompt: Estimate work-order defect risk using manufacturing.work_orders joined to manufacturing.defects for labels, manufacturing.machines for context and earlier manufacturing.sensor_readings for features. Keep post-start readings out of training features. Explain that manufacturing.defects are not unplanned machine-failure labels.

ideas.label: Handle the sensor data as it arrives
ideas.outcome: A pipeline that keeps up with the sensor feed and alerts on anomalies
ideas.prompt: Build a streaming pipeline over manufacturing.sensor_readings that keeps a rolling average per machine and raises something visible when a reading goes out of range. Prepared tables: manufacturing.machines.

ideas.label: Find where defects come from
ideas.outcome: A page ranking defects by machine, shift and plant
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard on manufacturing.defects joined to manufacturing.work_orders and manufacturing.machines: defect rate by machine, shift and plant, with contributors ranked. Aggregate each work order before joins to avoid multiplying produced units. The prepared data has no supplier field.

ideas.label: Work out who is about to cancel
ideas.outcome: A model that flags subscribers likely to leave
ideas.prompt: Create a subscriber-churn demo using media.subscriptions, media.viewers and media.churn_labels. Derive viewing features from media.view_events before each label observation date, excluding cancellation and later events from the predictors. Explain the synthetic-data limitations.

ideas.label: Recommend what to watch next
ideas.outcome: Personalised recommendations you can actually try out
ideas.prompt: Build a recommender over media.view_events and media.content, then let me type in a viewer id and see what it suggests and why. Prepared tables: media.viewers.

ideas.label: See what people are actually watching
ideas.outcome: A view of what is being watched, by whom and for how long
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over media.view_events and media.content: most-watched titles, completion rates, when people watch, and which titles get abandoned early.

ideas.label: Track how fast requests get resolved
ideas.outcome: A page showing service request volumes and how long they take
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over public_sector.service_requests: volume by category and area, how long each type takes to close, and which ones are ageing badly. Prepared tables: public_sector.facilities.

ideas.label: Make permits easy to look up
ideas.outcome: A searchable page for permits and their status
ideas.prompt: Build an app for searching public_sector.permits by address, type and status, showing where each one is in the process and how long it has been sitting there. Prepared tables: public_sector.facilities.

ideas.label: Ask where the budget went
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask budget questions in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over public_sector.budgets and public_sector.service_requests so I can ask how spending lines up with demand, in plain English.

ideas.label: Keep up with the smart meter feed
ideas.outcome: A pipeline that ingests meter readings continuously
ideas.prompt: Build a streaming pipeline over energy_utilities.meter_readings that aggregates consumption per meter per hour and handles readings that turn up late. Prepared tables: energy_utilities.meters.

ideas.label: See who is affected by outages
ideas.outcome: A page showing outages, how long they lasted and who they hit
ideas.prompt: Show outage duration and customers_affected from energy_utilities.outages by region. Summarise energy_utilities.meters and energy_utilities.customers separately for regional context; do not join individual energy_utilities.meters onto outage totals or claim an exact per-customer outage history.

ideas.label: Spot meters behaving strangely
ideas.outcome: A model that flags meters whose usage does not add up
ideas.prompt: Find energy_utilities.meters whose consumption pattern has shifted in a way that does not look like normal seasonal change. Build the baseline per meter, flag the outliers, and show me the most suspicious ones. Prepared tables: energy_utilities.meter_readings.

ideas.label: Work out which subscribers will leave
ideas.outcome: A model that flags subscribers likely to churn
ideas.prompt: Predict subscriber churn using call detail records, plan information and telco.churn_labels. Show me which behaviours predict it earliest and how much warning that gives. Prepared tables: telco.subscribers, telco.plans, telco.cdr.

ideas.label: Find the cells that are struggling
ideas.outcome: A page showing where the network is under strain
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over the call detail records and network cells: traffic per cell over time, dropped call rates, and which cells are consistently worst. Prepared tables: telco.cdr, telco.network_cells.

ideas.label: Ask whether people are on the right plan
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask about plans and usage in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over telco.subscribers, telco.plans and usage so I can ask which customers are on the wrong plan for how they actually use the service. Prepared tables: telco.cdr.

ideas.label: Work out which members are about to leave
ideas.outcome: A model that flags members likely to roll their balance to another fund
ideas.prompt: Predict which superannuation.members will roll out to another fund, using their balance, age, insurance cover and contribution history against superannuation.rollout_labels. Tell me which signals give the earliest warning, and be careful about the class imbalance - very few superannuation.members leave in any given period. Prepared tables: superannuation.contributions.

ideas.label: Ask about members and where their money sits
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask about balances and investment options in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over superannuation.members, their holdings and the investment options so I can ask things like which age groups are still in the default option, and how much of the fund sits in each option. Prepared tables: superannuation.member_holdings, superannuation.investment_options.

ideas.label: Check employer contributions are arriving
ideas.outcome: A pipeline that flags members whose employer has stopped paying
ideas.prompt: Build a pipeline over the superannuation.contributions data that works out each member's expected employer contribution rhythm and flags the ones where a payment looks late or missing. Check the data quality as it goes - I want to know if amounts are negative, dated in the future, or duplicated. Prepared tables: superannuation.members.

ideas.label: Work out which bookings will be cancelled
ideas.outcome: A model that flags bookings at risk of cancellation
ideas.prompt: Predict which travel.bookings get cancelled, using lead time, product type, channel and the customer's loyalty tier against travel.cancellation_labels. Show me how early the risk is visible and what it is worth - refunds are in the labels. Prepared tables: travel.customers.

ideas.label: See which trips are actually worth selling
ideas.outcome: A dashboard showing margin by destination, product and channel
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over the travel.bookings: gross value and margin by destination, product type and channel over time. Margin is thin on flights and better on packages, so make it obvious where the money really comes from rather than where the volume is. Prepared tables: travel.destinations.

ideas.label: Reconcile bookings against what was actually sold
ideas.outcome: A pipeline that surfaces bookings whose components do not add up
ideas.prompt: Build a medallion pipeline that joins travel.bookings to their travel.booking_items and checks the components reconcile against the booking value. Flag the ones that do not, and the unconfirmed items. Tell me how big the gap is rather than silently dropping the rows.

ideas.label: Work out which machines are about to fail
ideas.outcome: A model that flags assets heading for unplanned downtime
ideas.prompt: Predict unplanned asset failures from the sensor readings and operating hours against mining.failure_labels. Bearing temperature and vibration are the ones to watch. Failures are rare, so tell me what the model is worth in downtime hours avoided rather than just its accuracy. Prepared tables: mining.sensor_readings, mining.assets.

ideas.label: See how the sites are producing
ideas.outcome: A dashboard covering tonnes, grade and equipment availability by site
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over the daily production data: tonnes mined and shipped, head grade against target, equipment availability and unplanned downtime per site. Different mining.sites produce different commodities at very different tonnages, so make the comparison fair. Prepared tables: mining.production_daily.

ideas.label: Turn raw sensor data into something usable
ideas.outcome: A pipeline that aggregates asset telemetry and catches bad readings
ideas.prompt: Build a medallion pipeline over the sensor readings: raw through to hourly aggregates per asset, with data quality checks that catch impossible values and sensors that have gone quiet. I want to see how many readings get quarantined and why. Prepared tables: mining.sensor_readings, mining.assets.

ideas.label: See which loans are going bad
ideas.outcome: A dashboard ranking arrears by product, branch and vintage
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over the loan book and financial_services.arrears snapshots: financial_services.arrears rate and balance by product, branch and origination vintage. The snapshots are monthly, so show me which segments are getting worse rather than just which are worst today, and flag the hardship accounts separately. Prepared tables: financial_services.loans, financial_services.branches.

ideas.label: See how the business is doing
ideas.outcome: A revenue dashboard you can slice by product and time
ideas.prompt: Build a dashboard over the cross_industry.sales data: revenue and margin over time, best and worst cross_industry.products, and how the channels compare. Make the time period selectable. Prepared tables: cross_industry.customers.

ideas.label: See where people drop off
ideas.outcome: A funnel showing where visitors give up
ideas.prompt: Build a funnel over cross_industry.web_events grouped by session_id: viewed, searched, added to cart, checked out and purchased. Show the biggest drop-off. Treat purchase events as funnel events; do not claim to reconcile sales without a shared session key.

ideas.label: Ask questions about your customers
ideas.outcome: Somewhere you can ask about customers in plain English
ideas.prompt: Set up a Genie space over cross_industry.customers and cross_industry.sales so I can ask questions in plain English, with good column descriptions and a few examples to start from.

ideas.label: Predict who will buy again
ideas.outcome: A model scoring customers on how likely they are to come back
ideas.prompt: Build a model predicting which cross_industry.customers will buy again in the next 90 days, using how recently and how often they have bought and what they spent. Show me the top segment. Prepared tables: cross_industry.sales.

ideas.label: Build your first pipeline
ideas.outcome: A working pipeline with quality checks, explained as it goes
ideas.prompt: Build a small pipeline with quality checks over suitable prepared workshop data. Explain each useful step if I ask. If no prepared dataset fits, use a clearly labelled small sample.

ideas.label: Use my own data
ideas.outcome: Your own file loaded, explored and turned into a dashboard
ideas.prompt: I want to work with my own data. Walk me through getting a CSV or spreadsheet in here, then explore what is in it and build me a dashboard over the interesting parts.

ideas.label: Build a small internal tool
ideas.outcome: A working app your team could actually use, with a real URL
ideas.prompt: Build me a small internal tool as a Databricks App — something with a form, a list, and data that persists. Ask me what it should be for, then build it and deploy it.

ideas.label: Ask questions about your documents
ideas.outcome: An assistant that answers from documents you give it
ideas.prompt: Build a small assistant that answers from documents with citations. Explore the prepared workshop documents first. If none fit, use clearly labelled fictional documents and explain that limitation.
